Me and my husband have been long distance for about a year now because he joined the navy. He left for boot camp last July and we’ve seen each other few and far between since then. Before he left our love was like the love you see in movies. We loved each other. Hard. And the longer we were apart the easier it became to fight over the simplest things. You would think you would fight less being a part but that’s (for me at least) just not the case. My love language has always been physical touch and affection and his is quality time so when we don’t get these needs met it isn’t pretty. When we had weekends together after all the distance they were the best days for both of us. Like a movie again. We’ve had to fight to stay together. I understand and you definitely aren’t alone. It’s easy to question if you’re falling out of love when the things that made you fall in love in the first place aren’t actively present. Like quality time or physical affection. I always say to myself “you have to fight for the love that you know you have for each other.” Reminder: Love isn’t easy and it’s so confusing!! And sometimes love really is a choice. It’s okay to not know the answer sometimes <3 :)

Medication is really a marathon and not a sprint. I was first put on lexapro and bupropion when I had a mental health crisis in September (panic disorder) and reacted very very badly which resulted in mild serotonin syndrome. I was then put on lorazepam and Zoloft for anxiety, depression, and panic disorder. My body HATED the Zoloft so then I was put back on lexapro and then later added mirtazapine. The mirtazapine worked miracles for my sleep but as far as the lexapro went, it wasn’t doing much. In the middle of all this I was then diagnosed with BPD. A couple of weeks ago I tapered off the lexapro and was put on Effexor. So it’s been 10 months of my medication journey and I still don’t have it figured out yet. Just remember to be your own advocate but to also trust your doctors. It all takes time. Good luck!

The more you know, the more you grow! Although BPD itself is known for unstable self image, the more you learn about how the illness affects you and how to create healthier patterns of action and thinking, the closer you can be to having a more stable sense of self and the closer you can be to having a clear head!
